attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, given as an aside.

semantics.note: The normalised proposition drops the hedge "I daresay", which works as a softener (roughly "I suppose"). It also drops the "just a demo" framing and the aside's "story for another day" tone. It is a hedged forecast, not a firm commitment.

contract.note: The contract rightly treats this as a hedged prediction with no reliability threshold, no defined set of advertised capabilities and no deadline, so it sets no binary test. That is fair to the speaker's words.

reviews.rationale: "I daresay" qualifies the prediction, so under policy it is not scored. It also leaves "robustly" and "as advertised" undefined and has no deadline ("never"). The packet has no evidence items, and none could settle this without adding a standard the speaker never gave. Not adjudicable.

attribution.note: Marcus asserts the three incidents in his own voice. The board's "not consistently candid" phrase is quoted, but he endorses it as a pattern.

semantics.note: The normalised proposition captures the three alleged incidents. It leaves out the detail about the VC fund ownership, but the contract restores it.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair: "fudges" means a materially incomplete answer, and "lies" means knowingly false statements. Separating the components and the two readings of "owns" is reasonable. Only the ownership component depends on which reading is taken.

evidence.note: A dated transcript of the hearing. Altman flatly denied holding equity and did not mention any indirect interest or the fund.

OpenAI's own June 2023 disclosure admits an indirect interest through a YC fund. This shows the Senate answer left something out. It is a company disclosure, but it is an admission against the company's interest.

Altman's ownership of the Startup Fund ended with the March 29, 2024 filing. This contradicts "owns" if it means at publication. It also confirms he owned the fund at the time of the hearing, which supports the historical reading.

Toner's firsthand allegation of lying to the board. Its source_type label ("demonstration") is wrong. Under the contract an accusation alone does not establish knowing falsity, and the specific exchanges are not in the record.
Altman's denial, the statement under dispute. It is an interested party's statement and proves neither truth nor falsity.
WSJ chronology: Sky was recorded before the outreach to Johansson. This weakens the replacement inference but does not settle whether the resemblance was intended.

reviews.rationale: The Senate component holds: Altman said he had no equity, yet he had an indirect YC interest and owned the Startup Fund at the time (e1, e2, e3). Read as describing publication day, "owns" is wrong (e3). The Toner claim rests on her interested testimony without the underlying records, and the Johansson claim is not shown to be a knowing lie; the chronology cuts against it. Only the Senate fudge is supported. The rest is unsettled.
